PUBLISHERS NOTE

The late Mr. Simon Alexander Hewavitarane, who during his lifetime had begun to publish the Tripitaka, left a bequest for its completion after his death. He died suddenly on 17th January 1913, and in accordance with his wishes, his Trustees published the Commentaries on the Text in 49 volumes. After seventy years, these books are no longer readily available.

His widow, Mrs. Somawati Hewavitarane, who passed away on 10th January 1982 at the age of 94, had prior to her death established the Somawati Hewavitarane Trust to carry on the good work started by her late husband, and bequeathed her entire estate to this Trust.

We, the Trustees of the Somawati Hewavitarane Trust, having recognized the need to reprint the Commentaries, have undertaken this task to assist both students and teachers of the Dhamma. We hope that this act will help preserve the Noble Teachings of the Blessed One for the benefit of future generations, and thereby prolong the life of the Buddha Sasana for many more thousands of years.

May the fruits of this meritorious act benefit the late Simon Alexander Hewavitarane and Somawati Hewavitarane, Great Lay Devotee, throughout Samsara and toward their final attainment of Nibbana.

Noel Wijenaike
Nanda Amerasinghe
Parinda Ranasinghe

PREFATORY NOTE.

With the publication of the Sāratthasamuccaya or Catubhānavāraṭṭhakathā, I have much pleasure in placing before the public the 27th Volume of the Simon Hewavitarne Bequest Series. The editing of this volume has been done by the Venerable Doranegoda Pandita Nanasena Thero, Principal of the Vidyaraja Pirivena and member of the Tripitaka Publication Committee.

The proofs have been revised by the Venerable Kodagoda Upasena Maha Thero, Adhikarana Nayaka of the Ramañña Sect, Principal of Sri Saddharmodaya Pirivena, Panadura.

This Commentary appears to be a handbook compiled from the existing Commentaries of Buddhaghosa and Dhammapala, and adapted for use in this country by novices entering the monastic order. The author was a pupil of the Venerable Ananda Vanaratana Maha Thero of the Maha Vihara tradition, but his name is not known. A similar work is the Suttasangaha Commentary.

I am pleased to announce that the Samantapasadika Vinaya Commentary is ready for publication and will be released soon.

I wish to convey my heartfelt thanks to the Reverend Editor.

S. K. Moonesinghe.

PREFACE.

Like the pollen-circle of the sun, the Buddha, the great teacher who dispelled darkness, shines forth with the light of liberation — may this book, the essence of liberation, be rendered pure.

What is this called the Sārattha-samuccaya, the four-section explanatory commentary?

Answer: The commentary (atthakathā) here is that which accompanies the text, proceeding along with it, offering miscellaneous teachings here and there. That which was composed with the skill of twenty-two teachers, following the method of all languages taught together, was established here in Sinhala, in the Sinhala language, by one knowledgeable in the analytical method. It was written in the manner of exposition for the benefit of those who study the Buddha's teaching, by the Elder Dīpankara of Vāsi. Through this, the Sinhala people were enabled to understand. For indeed, the Elder of Buddhist learning had formerly composed in Sinhala a comprehensive exposition of the entire scripture. Some able persons commended it. Then, as time passed, it became scarce. The great Abhayasīlā assembly of practitioners declared: "It is not proper that this important Sinhala text should be unavailable — it should be reprinted." This itself was the basis for the matter. For the purpose of making basic commentary available, this work has been published. The Elder of Buddhist learning personally checked and corrected the text. Therefore it should be known: everything needed for the advancement of the Dhamma is provided herein. In this manner the publication has been prepared and released.

What is the purpose of this edition?

Answer: At the present time, the monastic community, beginning with the most senior pupils, teachers, and learned scholars, along with lay supporters, have an interest in Dhamma texts. Among them, some have shown readiness to study carefully. Thus the interest in Dhamma texts has grown. The measure of this is seen in the way the Dhamma is studied and practiced by all — thus it is said throughout.

[The passage, being a colophon-style text, discusses the composer's own teacher-lineage and the circumstances of composition.]

It is said that the kingship [of the text/work] is "Jayakilakambantisara," the illustrious one. He himself, out of respect for his teacher, [established the work] at Anuradhapura [or a similarly named monastic centre]. Having been instructed by his preceptor in the Dhamma and the monastic rule, he became his spiritual son. Thus it is said, at the time of explaining the stanza establishing the text:

"For one who has accomplished the practice of concentration,
For one skilled in composition and inquiry,
For one devoted to the bliss of the Buddha's teaching,
This effort toward establishing the text is for great merit.

For one who, through the practice beginning with virtue,
Has students, companions, and good friends,
For one who delights in asceticism without craving,
The 'Padasadhana' is declared for one of good conduct." Thus.

This treatise on the method of establishing words is said by some to have been composed for the sake of [his] teacher's joy. That should be understood as the standard. He who [composed it] was renowned as one learned in the Buddha's word and the Buddhist discipline; for that reason he became known by the name "Ananda" (joy). In this way, having completed [the work] for the sake of the growth of the elders' tradition, [he] was praised by the wise as one who, through proper conduct, benefited his teacher's lineage. It is said that this undertaking was done out of devotion to his preceptor, and so it is declared:

"This great and vast ocean of knowledge
Brings joy and delight to the wise." Thus.

In this way the village-folk proclaim his fame. Even so, among the wise councillors there, some, out of partiality, did not wish to give full credit to [this] work of joy. The compilers of the various schools, together with the teachers of the various traditions, united in a common agreement, discoursed together on the structure of the commentaries, dividing the subject matter among the joyous treatise's sections. Their various interpretations could not [all] be taken as standard; thus some, for the sake of their own satisfaction, elevated certain portions improperly. Other scholars of differing views did not accept such alterations. Therefore, in these matters, some teachers, acting improperly, are to be understood as having strayed from the tradition. Thus it should be known.

He who is the venerable Hewavitarana Mahashaya, bearer of the entire Tipitaka, having kept alive the glory of the teaching without interruption — the one who fulfilled the wishes of those in the world — the custodian of the Tipitaka manuscripts, the chief patron C. J. Hewavitarana Mahashaya, through the merit he had accumulated, in the fifty-eighth year, caused the fundamental texts of the brotherhood of elders to be published and set forth. Through effort and dedication, having fulfilled the great wish, he accomplished what was dear to his heart. Did Mara the evil one, who hinders the dispensation, try to obstruct? Those great brotherhood of elders, having overcome all those hindrances and obstacles, attained their goal. Having accomplished this through the Tipitaka treasury, making it available for study, through the great Dhamma treasury — may the Triple Gem protect all, be it so, truly.

That the Tipitaka may be studied in the monastery,
Written with one's own hand with clear mindfulness,
That it may protect the people in all directions —
May it be so through the grace of Hewavitarana.

Verses of Homage:

1. Born in the village of Hiriyāla, of noble family,
Of the distinguished Sinhala race, of noble birth.

2. Having crossed the ocean of samsara, having renounced sensual pleasures in form,
A support to the dispensation, known among the wise.

3. Having served the good dispensation, O great Elder,
Foremost in wisdom, noble in the highest degree.

4. Having caused the ancient Pali texts to be illuminated,
Rightly and properly established them in their place.

5. Having lived a life of virtue in the village of Suttanga,
Protected by the wise, his merit pure and clear.

6. Victorious like the great sun, radiant with glory,
Unwavering in kindness to all beings everywhere.

7. Of that teacher's lineage, of supreme conduct,
Following in the great elder's path of Suttanga.

9. One who brings people together, who reveals the Dhamma unceasingly, who is virtuous and worthy of veneration by the faithful.

10. One who is uplifted in spirit, who has mastered the texts, who dwells in an environment adorned with glory.

11. One accomplished in the ways of the community, who oversees the conduct of the order, protecting and guiding those under his care.

12. One who is learned in the Pandava tradition, who is calm in mind, who lives in an environment of wisdom and peace.

13. In the village of Deranagoda, the sage and sage-like one dwells, worthy of veneration by the assembly of the faithful.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

He who for a long time cultivated the elimination of mental defilements through inner development,
taught with compassion, revered by those who heard his teaching.

The ancient ones brought together all that dispels obstacles,

gathered in one place, respectfully arranged.

The names of the Nikaya-compendiums are as follows:

"The Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, and the Abhidhamma collection —
these five Nikayas constitute the Dhamma in its entirety."

The discourses of the Digha Nikaya are the long discourses; the Majjhima Nikaya consists of the middle-length discourses; the Samyutta Nikaya consists of the connected discourses grouped by topic; the Anguttara Nikaya consists of discourses arranged numerically in increasing order.

The Khuddakapatha, Dhammapada, Udana, Itivuttaka, Suttanipata, Vimanavatthu, Theragatha, Therigatha, Jataka, Niddesa, Patisambhida, Apadana, Buddhavamsa, Cariyapitaka, and the Vinayapitaka and Abhidhammapitaka — all the remainder beyond the four Nikayas is called the Khuddaka Nikaya.

Sārattha-samuccaya

Why is it called the "Buddhas' Assembly" (Buddhānikāya)? Because it is the dwelling-place and gathering of many Buddhas assembled together, and because of that assembled dwelling it is called a nikāya (collection/assembly).

"Even in a single assembly I do not perceive any sound, just as creatures go in search of livelihood" — in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Vikallanikāya, and so on, such terms appear in the world in connection with the Teaching.

Now the Going for Refuge, the Ten Training Rules, the qualities of a novice — associated with the Ratana Sutta, the Kāraṇīya-metta Sutta, and related texts — have been placed here under the heading of the Buddhakkhanda. They are arranged with the Metta Sutta and related texts: the Metta Sutta comes under the heading of the Theragāthā-nikāya; and from the Saṃyutta Nikāya comes the Isigili Sutta; from the Dīgha Nikāya the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta is drawn. These suttas having been cited from their respective nikāyas, the Isigili Sutta is taken for reference. In this same way the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, the Metta Sutta, the Dhaja Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta — by means of these, it is said, recitation should be performed.

This having been arranged, in order to show the sequence of these selected suttas, I now take up the explanation, beginning with the phrase: "I go for refuge to the Buddha — and so forth — I go for refuge."

The summary matrix of topics in the following section is:

Why and by whom was this Going for Refuge spoken?
Why was it spoken as it was, and why in this particular order from the beginning?

Having clarified the basis and the preliminary matter up to that point,
let one illuminate the meaning of Going for Refuge to the Buddha.

Let one illuminate each cause and condition point by point,
and the method of the Dhamma refuge — that is the approach here.

Let one indicate the reasons with precision,
and illuminate the Going for Refuge with similes.

Now first of all, regarding this Going for Refuge — by whom was it spoken, how was it spoken, where was it spoken, when was it spoken, and why was it spoken thus, and from what beginning? Let us examine this carefully. As to who spoke it — was it spoken by the Blessed One? Yes, it was spoken by the Blessed One, not by a disciple, not by a seer, not by a god. Where? At Isipatana in the Deer Park at Bārāṇasī. For what purpose? Because those companions who had previously been with the Blessed One...

Saranavannana (Commentary on the Refuges)

For the welfare of many, for the happiness of the world, the Dhamma is being taught by the One worthy of offerings. What is comparable? Those who have gone forth and those who have received higher ordination, as follows: "Thus, monks, having taught the teaching, having given full ordination, having first addressed them with words of good counsel, having caused them to sit at the feet of monks, having had them learn by heart — in this way, having been thus instructed, they go to the Buddha for refuge, to the Dhamma for refuge, to the Sangha for refuge."

Why is it called the "Kassamo" etc.? In this ninefold training, as found in the three Pitakas among the sacred texts, as set forth by the noble ones of old, gods and humans become lay followers or those who have gone forth, and thus the teaching supports them. In the origin story relating to the Buddhas, this has been stated at the beginning — this is the explanation of that beginning. What does "hidananokkhana" mean? What has now been stated as "Taking refuge in the Excellent One, in the community" — this too is without a further basis. Having crossed beyond the floods of passion, having attained liberation of mind, and being free from the cycle of existence, those who are truly established in the teaching are led to the cessation of suffering. Thus the Buddha — the Awakened One — the Blessed One...

[The page begins mid-discussion of a commentary explaining the various meanings of the word "paññā" (wisdom).]

"Paññā" means: by means of understanding, one awakens to the entire body of wholesome qualities beginning with virtue—thus it is said; by the accomplishment of understanding all phenomena, one is said to awaken—thus it is said; by means of understanding, without having been instructed by another, one awakens by oneself to that which was not understood—thus it is said; by means of special understanding, one who discerns persons of various qualities is said to understand—thus it is said; by means of understanding, one who has removed delusion regarding a single matter without difficulty, and who is freed from all defilements, is said to understand—thus it is said; the one who has ascended to the "single path" is, by understanding, called by that name of the path he went by—thus it is said; by understanding, having reached the highest, supreme self-awakening, one is called fully awakened, one of awakened nature; having himself attained the unsurpassed, one is called of awakened nature—thus it is said. The state of not-yet-awakened understanding and the attainment of awakening by understanding, the nature of awakening, are called synonyms of "bodhi" (awakening). Owing to the combination of blue gems, there is a "blue colour" and a "gem colour"; likewise thereafter, by combination with one quality, one is designated by understanding. By understanding, that quality is named; this is set out in the context of the meaning of wisdom (paññā). This explanation should be understood by the wise in this manner, in the way described—thus the eye [of wisdom should see it].

Now, as to going for refuge and the rest: the meaning of "harming" is this—by refuge, by the going for refuge, by refuge-going, suffering, doubt, mental distress, and misery are allayed, removed, and set at rest. Fear and danger from unwholesome destinations, which are opposed to one's good, are restrained thereby—thus it is called "harming" [of the perils]. By such practice, by resorting in this way, one has freedom from distress. This is the detailed explanation. This proliferation, this manifold explanation, this exposition rendered elaborate, dispels affliction, enables the practice and continuation of right effort, and brings about the various kinds of refuge-going together with their distinctions. Of these, one should understand it thus: thus and thus is refuge-going, thus and thus is its meaning; by this exposition, they are understood accordingly.

[Therein, it is said:] "From this day forth, those lay followers who approach for refuge, declaring, 'We go to the teacher, to the doctrine, and to the community of monks as our refuge'"—in the manner of the ascetics Tapassu and Bhallika who first took refuge, and the deity Sakka who said, "We go to the master as refuge"—thus, and the great assembly which said, "We go to you, Venerable Gotama, as refuge"—in such fashion, the going for refuge by various people on various occasions should here be understood in detail.

"Whatever is found among those, what has been told and described and laid down in common,

those training rules set down are to be practiced accordingly.

Among those of common scope, for those of common sharing,

Having abandoned those roots of greed and so forth, through the practice of root-cutting,

These ten training precepts beginning with abstention from killing living beings were spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by disciples; and they were spoken as being blameworthy. At the Jetavana monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika, after having the Venerable Rāhula go forth, [the Buddha] established the training precepts for novices (sāmaṇera) as applicable to all without exception.

This has been said thus:-

"Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavatthu as long as he wished, set out wandering towards Sāvatthī. Wandering by stages, he in due course arrived at Sāvatthī and dwelt there in the Jetavana monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Now at that time it occurred to the novices: 'How many training precepts should we undertake?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One allowed the novices ten training precepts, in which they should train, namely: abstention from killing living beings ... up to ... abstention from the basis for heedlessness through intoxicants."

These are the training precepts referred to. In accordance with what has been said [elsewhere], just as in taking the three refuges, so too in accordance with the ten training precepts, one undertakes the precept of abstention from killing living beings and so forth — this should be understood in general terms.

Here, as to whether these are shared [in common with the precepts of lay devotees] or not, it should be said: these [precepts], starting from the very first one mentioned, are common to both lay devotees and novices by way of moral virtue (sīla); but as for the Uposatha precepts, for lay devotees the seventh factor differs somewhat. Thus, while in general they are held in common, when it comes to actual practice the novices have certain distinctive features that should be observed as common only in a general sense.

Regarding the matter of the five precepts: such things as abstention from killing living beings are said to be "in accordance with nature" (pakatisikkhā) in the case of what is natural, or to be "in accordance with convention" in other cases; the abstentions should be understood accordingly. Since one states "I undertake the training precept of abstention from...", this expression is common throughout; a distinction between what is to be distinguished and what is common should be understood in this way.

First, with regard to "abstention" (veramaṇī): one who, having approached a state in which enmity could arise through the body, speech, or mind towards a being, refrains from that — such a person is said to be "one who abstains." The precept of such a one's restraint is called the "precept of abstention." It is called a "training precept" (sikkhāpada) because it is the basis for what is to be trained — "sikkhā" meaning that which should be trained, and "pada" meaning the basis on which one approaches it; thus "sikkhāpada" — this is the etymological derivation.

"By what is one said to abstain?" it is said; abstention in the sense of undertaking (samādāna) is, first of all, the release of oneself or another from unwholesome states such as killing living beings and so on. What is the reason for this? By that very means by which one abstains. Abstention through attainment (samāpatti) is wholesome in the manner stated. What is the reason? Because of taking killing and so forth as object.

As for intoxicants such as liquor and spirits, one who has undertaken the precepts abstains from the basis of heedlessness that is liquor and spirits. In the case of a monk who must bring forth such matters, [the text continues discussing] that one with the precepts [observes] inconceivable wisdom and so forth, and thereby maintains the holy life free from killing living beings. Here again, regarding this very matter, [the question arises] whether one who does not give what is not given, having known that something belongs to another, takes it with the thought "let it be taken" and thus knows it as such -- or whether, not knowing it clearly, but merely taking what belongs to another with excessive desire, one takes it, thinking "let it be taken" while not truly knowing -- whereby one speaks of abstention from the unwholesome state of one's own killing of living beings. This is stated. Why? Because of the various objects it concerns, it is to be understood as external.

In the analytical exposition of the training precepts, the wise discern the precepts category by category -- and so on -- to understand which practices conduce to wholesomeness, being associated with the object of happiness and well-being as cause, or with the object of right understanding (bodhi) as cause; this is the cause stated as the object of right understanding. By this, the abstention from the unwholesome state of killing one's own is not obstructed in respect of restraint. But regarding what was earlier said -- whether knowingly taking what is not given, with the thought "let it be taken," one truly knows, or whether, without resolve, merely from habitual tendency, not clearly knowing, one does not truly understand -- this remains open to further explanation.

Thus the precepts, difficult to attain, are hard for beings subject to suffering,
Exemplified for the wise, [as declared by] the great sage, the Noble Person.

Thus ends the exposition to be understood regarding the varieties of abstention.

"Hell" refers to that state wherein beings who commit the fivefold evil deed of killing go to, being overcome by harsh and immediate results consistent with the nature of such kamma, in both this life and lives to come, bound as it were to unwholesome destinies. Moreover, one who is of impure mind and intent on killing living beings becomes, as it were, no longer counted among human beings, being deprived of the merit of human existence. Thus is to be understood the classification concerning the nature and condition of such wrongdoing. Furthermore, through abstention from killing living beings and such precepts, the classification based on the origin of feeling as root of action is also to be discerned with wisdom.

What is meant by "to be discerned with wisdom"? It means that the arising of that very abstention occurs through bodily volition, bodily intention, verbal intention, or the intention combining both body and speech. That same [abstention], arising together with pleasant feeling, constitutes wholesome bodily action, likewise arising together with pleasant feeling; similarly rooted in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion -- rooted thus in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. The remaining types, moreover, concern bodily action, abstention from false speech as verbal action, and mental action rooted likewise, arising together accordingly.

Now, in this section, the wisdom by which these things are to be fully comprehended — in order to show the manner of its arising in terms of the subject matter of the meditation on what has come by way of the path, and to produce the arising of things not previously known in all their aspects that are beyond the scope of those suttas — the Blessed One declared: "One thing, O bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated leads to great disenchantment, to great benefit, to great security from bondage, to great mindfulness and clear comprehension, to the acquisition of knowledge and vision, to pleasant abiding here and now, to the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation. What is that one thing? It is mindfulness of the body. Those bhikkhus who do not partake of the deathless — they do not partake of mindfulness of the body. Those who partake of mindfulness of the body partake of the deathless. For those in whom mindfulness of the body is undeveloped — it is undeveloped; cultivated — it is cultivated; neglected — it is neglected; not neglected — it is not neglected; rarely practiced — it is rare; energetically practiced — it is energetically practiced, for those in whom mindfulness of the body has been aroused." Thus the Blessed One, in many ways, instructed: "How, O bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu develop mindfulness of the body? Here, O bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward, enclosed by skin, full of various kinds of impurity: 'There are in this body: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin...'" — thus named and taught in full by the Blessed One through many analytical classifications of mindfulness of the body, arranged in a systematic compendium — this is the arousing of mindfulness. This section of the commentary explains the "Thirty-two Parts of the Body" meditation. It states that some teachers classify these parts in different groupings — some count certain constituents together under one heading, others separate them further, depending on common characteristics such as location, color, consistency or function. For example, parts such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and skin are grouped by their external, visible nature, while flesh, sinews, bones, and marrow are grouped by their internal character. The text details how the kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, and mesentery relate to one another in sequence, describing the body as a continuous chain of interconnected organs.

It further addresses an objection: why is it that one who contemplates the heart may or may not also perceive the liver, the diaphragm, or other adjoining organs within the same act of attention? The commentary explains that perception of one part does not necessarily entail simultaneous perception of another; a practitioner may attend to the heart alone, or to the heart together with the liver, and so on, according to the way the mind settles upon each item in the sequence of contemplation. This should be understood as a general principle applicable throughout the thirty-two-part enumeration, the remaining parts to be treated by analogy with what has been explained.

The passage closes by noting how such contemplation reveals that nothing in the body possesses an "owner" or a self that grasps and knows — the sinews, bones, and flesh do not themselves perceive or desire; rather, one who truly sees in this way goes beyond conceit and craving, and such insight is said to be a mark of understanding (paññā) that leads toward liberation.

54 Sārattha-samuccaya

Those who reckon signs such as branches and so forth do not use water according to the flow of sound. But when distributions are made, having dismissed that sign, without giving it further attention, they use water and other things as a basis for purification. In the same way, regarding hair of the head, body hair, and other components of nutriment, we do not see these as supporting the Dhamma, nor do we regard them with pleasure. With respect to hair of the head and similar unlovely things, taking them up for the purpose of perceiving their foulness — that is the usage. Having dismissed the notion of "mine" or "self," and cultivating attention to foulness and the like, one thinks: "This is the Dhamma of foulness and the like; this is to be contemplated; why should it be colored in? Why should it be cleaned?" And again: "Why should one strive to regard what is foul as beautiful? Why should it be cleaned and purified?" It was said: "The color of hair, seen in its place, is not [truly] beautiful when perceived through foulness." Having seen it through the perception of foulness, one attends to it with the mind. What then of the hair of the head? — it is supremely repulsive in the highest degree, disgusting, revolting to humans and gods alike, neither food for eating nor fit to be consumed; whether in the light of day or otherwise, hair is among those things that are truly disgusting and unpleasant to contemplate. Considered in terms of the perception of foulness, hair is repulsive in origin, in nature, and in conclusion — not fit for food or enjoyment by day or night. Likewise with body hair — it is repulsive, and in the highest sense it is wholly disagreeable. For one who has recognized this in the bodies of others and in oneself, knowing it to be associated with bones, skin, and sinews, it is thoroughly unappealing. For one who contemplates it with mindfulness, the human body, examined carefully and analytically, is seen to be not truly beautiful or worthy of delight. Thus, with attention directed toward foulness, that foulness is established in the mind; and again, through verbal description, foulness is established in the mind. When sound is attended to, it is attended to in the mind. Thus, the mind attending to sound, to verbal description, and to the full range of the Dhamma — this is the sequence. Following the sequence of mindfulness of the body up to foulness, it is established in the mind. Following the sequence of mindfulness to the highest point, the mind is likewise established. Thus, from the mind being established, verbal expression also becomes established in the Dhamma. Accordingly, when the sequence of mindfulness of the body is followed by one whose mind is established in foulness, he gains through the Tathāgata's teaching an unshaken foothold in that place, and so it is said.

By making use of alms-food, I ward off the old feeling [of hunger] and do not produce a new one. Thus there will be for me a righteous manner of living, a blameless life, and comfort. Where they do not cause illness through improper sights and such things that are unsuitable, and one uses the dwelling with a spirit of solitude and dispassion — the monk should understand this as the "proper use of dwelling-places and climate conditions."

Regarding the examination of lodgings, illness-related matters, the treatment of disease, the use of requisites, and their practice: the basis of all this is robes. The taking up of robes is the most basic. The monk's robe-use and lodging are closely related. Requisites for the one gone forth include: it is said "for the city-dweller such and such requisites are proper." "Many kinds of tools and implements" are mentioned as items for those in various vocations. "These are the life-requisites of the renunciants" — this is also said. Both "attendant upon" and "surrounding" are meant here. The life of the monk together with these life-requisites is maintained and protected. Because of this, what is called a requisite is indeed a requisite. Thus the examination of lodgings and their requisites — requisites for the examination of lodgings — this examination of lodgings and its requisites. Among those who govern and examine: medicines, robes, and similar life-requisites are what is meant. **For the knowing of what is to be known, for the abandoning of what is to be abandoned. What is called illness** — those such as relatives, and "from where would that which is not given come?" — these are called illness. The arising of illness, the feeling of suffering, the feeling of unwholesome results — these are the feelings of illness. **The highest purpose** is the highest cessation of suffering; "may this being who suffers be freed from suffering" — such is the spirit herein.

As for the meaning of this word, it should be understood that "thus was it heard by me" — this phrase establishes what was heard as pure and well‑apprehended, and this explanation shows its purity by way of the method of correct reasoning. Herein, this section explains what should be heard as purified, as stated by one who has the wisdom of enlightenment regarding this. The word "sutta" (heard) shows the state of being heard through the faculty of hearing, together with its proper apprehension. "Then" (tadā) indicates the function of the organ of hearing engaging with its object. Herein is shown its own particular characteristic. "Heard" indicates the state of sound-hearing. "Then" indicates the explanation of what has been pointed out. Herein is the full exposition with its wisdom-based explanation.

[Then follows discussion of] "at one time" and its various possible interpretations — a time reckoned by years, months and so on; or the particular occasion when the Blessed One was teaching the gods and showing forth the extraordinary; or the occasion of the destruction of darkness in regard to that teaching; the occasion of the union of that teaching with concentration — one occasion; the occasion of accomplishment in compassion together with the welfare of beings according to the Dhamma being taught — thus it is called "one occasion." The meaning is "at a particular time." This refers to a time connected with special circumstances.

At that time, the Blessed One, having taught this discourse in just this way, on exactly that occasion dwelt in compassion thus. Now, the explanation of the greatness of the word "Bhagavā," expressing the completeness of his virtues, comes next:-

"The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent; 'Bhagavā' is the best of words. Since he is worthy of the highest reverence, he is therefore called 'Bhagavā.'"

Herein, concerning its etymological elaboration [various meanings are given] regarding how this designation of "Bhagavā" came to be applied to the Blessed One — by the Buddhas of the past, it has been conferred by way of a name established through supreme wisdom. As the Venerable Sāriputta Thera has said: "'Bhagavā' is not a name given by a mother, father, brother, sister, friend, companion, kinsman or blood relation... this designation 'Bhagavā' is the final epithet of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they attain omniscient knowledge at the foot of the Bodhi tree, realized together with the attainment of that knowledge." Thus is it said. Moreover, in order to proclaim his virtues, these verses are recited:-

"He has broken, destroyed, and overcome [defilements]; he approaches, having divided and analyzed. He is endowed with good fortune, he has frequented and cultivated [the path] abundantly. Thus, on account of these, he is called 'Bhagavā.'"

The explanation already given in the Niddesa should be understood in this same way. But here is another sequence of synonymous explanations:-

"'Bhagavā' is one who has broken; happily has he gone forth, having abandoned by division. Having destroyed, he dwells master of all things — thus is he 'Bhagavā.'"

As for the change of vowel-sound and the elision of a syllable here, this is a feature of grammatical derivation, which occurs on account of euphony or by analogy with irregular derivative forms (pisodarādi), since, being endowed with both mundane and supramundane qualities such as giving, virtue, and so forth, together with the perfections — the Blessed One is thus called "Bhagavā." Thus should the word "Bhagavā" be understood.

The word "Bhagavā" is explained thus: And so the rest of the words are to be understood in the same way. The Blessed One has abandoned all evil states — thus he is called Bhagavā. Because he has dispersed and driven away the three kinds of fortune, he is Bhagavā. Various explanations have been given by various teachers. And so it was said: as far as the directions extend — east, west, and so forth — he is called Bhagavā.

Now in order to show the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One, which is to be taught and realized, this statement was made: "At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling..." At such a time, the Blessed One, having become accomplished in his form of the Noble Dhamma, was ready to teach. Thus it is that such a teacher of the Noble Dhamma, the bearer of the ten powers, having conquered all adversaries, having overcome all hardships, generates enthusiasm for the teaching. Thus the sermon is established properly. The phrase "a certain time" indicates proper occasion; "the Monk community" indicates proper disciples; "Bhagavā" indicates the proper teacher. "Sāvatthī" — this refers to the city of that name, renowned in all directions — thus it is called Sāvatthī.

The learned teachers further say: what is the cause that this city is praised and called Sāvatthī? Various explanations exist. Some say:

"Sāvatthī, gathering together all excellent things,
is foremost among cities in all respects.

The beautiful city of the Kosalans, charming to behold, delightful,
shining and brilliant, famous and unequalled, destroyer of suffering.

Fortunate, full of splendor, victorious, supremely delightful,
supreme among the cities of the gods" — and so on.

Thus Sāvatthī is praised in the Samajana. "Viharati" (he was dwelling) — without distinction, among the noble dwellings fit for a supreme noble one, and so he dwells there. The Blessed One's dwelling while standing, walking, sitting, or lying down should all be understood thus. Therefore the word "inspection" is appropriate here, and it has been correctly said by the elders.

It is said that one alone takes delight in dwelling apart from wrong view and remains undefiled. Thus, in each and every one, the path of mindfulness is fulfilled through the body. Herein, "superior to human states," meaning the states beyond ordinary men — these refer to the noble ones' attainments, the states of the Ariyans, the states associated with the ten wholesome courses together with the attainments of the Ariyans, and the superior Dhamma — this teaching exists among and belongs to such distinguished persons; it does not exist among, nor belong to, ordinary worldlings.

In "the knowledge and vision of surpassing distinction," the knowledge here refers to the supramundane wisdom — insight that arises from vision; "vision" here means the noble eye of wisdom that perceives the true nature of things; it is the full understanding attained through the stages of the noble path. Just as the human state (mentioned previously) refers to states associated with the Ariyan path, so too "the knowledge and vision of distinction" refers to the purified wisdom-vision belonging to one liberated from defilements, who has attained the highest superior human state. Thus "superior human states" here are used synonymously with the collective attainments comprising the noble states.

"The knowledge and vision of distinction" refers to the purified wisdom and vision of one freed from defilements. "Attainment" (adhigama) means "obtaining." "Why is this so?" is asked regarding the particular instance of attainment. "At the time of death," in the fifth sense, refers to the moment of dying. "Previously," with reference to a particular attainment already accomplished — such a person, not having fallen away from that attainment at the moment of death, is said to have "not fallen" in that specific sense, and this is named accordingly in that context. "These ten dhammas" refers to the teaching expressing the collection of these states. As stated in sequence, the explanation here proceeds in brief summary form.

"Birth" here, in this discourse, refers likewise [to the corresponding meaning]. "From that" refers to the arising of joy and happiness etc. "Reflection" denotes the noble lineage — from the descent and rebirth [of the Bodhisatta], together with the subsequent recollection in accordance with this discourse. Now, as to the Mangala Sutta that is to be explained next — this discourse on the ten kammas has been placed here because it deals with the attainment of states superior to the ordinary human condition through going forth and taking refuge, by way of accomplishment in virtue and so forth among the tenfold wholesome courses — hence, by way of connection in meaning, the teaching of blessings (mangala) was placed immediately following this discourse. 70 Sārattha-samuccaya

It is said that in Jambudīpa, in various cities, markets, assemblies and the like, great numbers of people gathered together and, having given gold and silver, debated over a period of four months what was auspicious. Then one man from among those assembled asked: "What is called auspicious? What is seen as auspicious? What is heard as auspicious? What is perceived as auspicious? Who is auspicious by birth?" At this, a man called "one who holds birth to be auspicious" said: "I was born auspiciously; the world is auspicious through birth; birth is what is reckoned as most auspicious. Form — that is to say, hearing at a favorable time the call of a bird speaking at the right moment — such as one who is like a wood-apple, or a young boy, or one bearing a full vessel, or one going to the right, or one carrying an Āraja, or one of good conduct, or one of the Kāpila lineage, or any such form reckoned as supremely auspicious in form — this I declare to be auspicious by birth." His words were approved by some. Some did not approve. Those who did not approve fell into dispute with him.

Then a man called "one who holds what is heard to be auspicious" said: "What is called 'hearing' is neither beautiful nor ugly — it applies equally to the lovely and the unlovely, to one's mother and to one who is not one's mother. If birth alone were auspicious, then everything would be auspicious. Therefore birth is not the auspicious thing. Rather, what is heard is auspicious. 'Heard' means that which is reckoned as supremely auspicious in the domain of sound — hearing at a favorable moment names such as Vaḍḍhī, Vaḍḍhamānā, Puṇṇā, Pussā, Sumatī, Sirī, Sirivaḍḍhā, or today a relation being born, a joyful gathering, a good day, a fortunate occasion, a sound reckoned as supremely auspicious — this I declare to be 'auspicious by hearing.'" His words also were approved by some. Some did not approve. Those who did not approve fell into dispute with him.

Then a man called "one who holds what is smelled to be auspicious" said: "What is that thing called 'hearing'? Whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, whether from one's mother or not from one's mother, it is merely heard. If what is heard were auspicious, then everything would be auspicious. Therefore hearing is not the auspicious thing. Rather, what is smelled is auspicious. 'Smelled' means that which purifies and is reckoned as auspicious — such as smelling at a favorable moment lotuses or other flowers scattered about, or one who brings sweet-smelling food, or one who touches fresh green herbs, or one who touches moist things, or fragrant things, or one touching something fragrant, or one bearing a garland of flowers, a basket of fragrant things, or one carrying perfumes, or anything of such a form reckoned as supremely auspicious — that which has the quality of a sweet fragrance, at a favorable time, smelling something of the nature of a sweet fragrance — this I declare to be 'auspicious by smell.'" His words also were approved by some. Some did not approve. Now the one who held birth to be auspicious and the one who held hearing to be auspicious began to dispute —

They did not allow each other's view. Among those people, those who held that visible things (ditthamangalika) were auspicious held that only the visible constituted the auspicious sign. Those who held that heard or cognized things (sutamutamangalika) were auspicious held that only the heard and cognized were the auspicious sign. In this way, the question of the auspicious sign became known throughout the entire continent of Jambudipa.

Then throughout the whole of Jambudipa, people gathered in crowds and debated: "This is the auspicious sign!" "No, this is the auspicious sign!" The guardian deities of those people, having heard the debate among their people, likewise argued among themselves. The friendly deities of those guardian deities also joined in. Then the sky-dwelling deities, who were friends of those deities, also took up the debate. And the deities who travel on the wind, friends of the sky-dwelling deities, likewise argued. In this same way, the debate spread all the way up to the Akanittha (highest) deities, with groups upon groups of deities gathered and debating "This is the auspicious sign!" Thus the uproar over the auspicious sign spread throughout the ten-thousand world-systems. Even though people debated which was the auspicious sign, not one person was found who could definitively settle the matter. Thus the Mangala-uproar (mangala-kolahala) arose in the world. There are five kinds of uproar (kolahala): the world-cycle uproar (kappa-kolahala), the wheel-turning monarch uproar (cakkavatti-kolahala), the Buddha uproar (buddha-kolahala), the auspicious sign uproar (mangala-kolahala), and the paccekabuddha uproar (moneyya-kolahala).

Among these, the deities of the sense-sphere realm, with disheveled hair, weeping faces, tear-stained cheeks, wearing various strange garments, travel through hundreds of thousands of world-systems announcing: "A world-cycle is coming to an end — this world will be destroyed, the great ocean will dry up, Mount Sineru and the great mountains will be shattered and destroyed — the world's destruction approaches. Therefore, dear friends, cultivate compassion, loving-kindness; cherish your mothers, cherish your fathers; honor the elders of your families; be diligent, do not be heedless!" — and thus they inform humankind. This is called the world-cycle uproar (kappa-kolahala). Those same sense-sphere deities announce that a wheel-turning monarch will arise in the world, and inform humankind accordingly. This is called the wheel-turning monarch uproar (cakkavatti-kolahala). Then those same deities, together with the earth-dwelling deities, announce throughout hundreds of thousands of world-systems that a Buddha will arise in the world, and inform humankind accordingly. This is called the Buddha uproar (buddha-kolahala). Then those same deities announce to gods and humans throughout the world-systems that a certain auspicious observance will be proclaimed, and inform humankind accordingly. This is called the auspicious sign uproar (mangala-kolahala).

That same deva asked, "Where will this matter dwell?" Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, having resolved their question, concluded this discourse.

Commentary on the Madhyala Sutta (Mangala Sutta)

This exposition commences in this manner, in accordance with the tradition handed down since the time it was first stated. In the context of the great "ten-dwelling" discourse, the commentary proceeds. In elaborating on this matter, the exposition is grounded in that which is appropriate for the understanding of the middling disposition.

We shall here undertake the exposition. How so? "Atha" is spoken in relation to what is undetermined. "Me" refers to that spoken with authority, arising in one's own perception. By this, it indicates that in the Blessed One's presence this exposition arose. Why is this said? Because it is said without specifying a particular reference, by way of that very designation.

The deity alone is twofold, being held in common. But here, when referring to one particular deity, the phrase is used of that which inhabits uncommonly. "Atikkanta ratiya" (of surpassing radiance) refers to one of excelling radiance; by that, it is said as "of surpassing and shining radiance." "Atikkanta-vannam" here means possessing surpassing beauty, of excelling complexion, of radiant appearance, distinguishing from the ordinary. By that it is called "possessed of excelling, luminous form."

"Kevalakappam" means wholly, in entirety, with nothing remaining — "entirely and exhaustively," possessing a complete sense, thus it stands as "pervading entirely" and so forth, in this manner it was said. "Obhaseti" means illuminating like the moon, like the sun, making luminous all around — this is the sense.

"So the Blessed One approached" — meaning performing the deed of approaching; by this it is said "approached" to signify the Blessed One's going near. The meaning is thus established: that through this deed, the Blessed One is said to have "approached." By this word, the sense that the Blessed One approached in splendor through deity-power is thereby conveyed.

Having thus understood through this reasoning, this account was transmitted by various compilers and committed to certain forms, as the recollection of one grasping as if gathering gathered flowers. "Upasankami" (approached) is said with this reasoning. "Upasankamitva" means having gone up to the point of approach, and from there having gone further — to the point of being near, reaching the presence of the Blessed One, is what is said. Having approached the Blessed One, worshipped the Blessed One, paid reverence, saluted, stood respectfully aside. "Ekamantam" means in one direction, to one side, standing apart. Or, "ekamantam" means "near" or "in close proximity" to the Blessed One.

"Atthasi" means having completed the approach, having bowed and stood; having bowed, stood at one side — thus it is understood. Standing respectfully, bowed, that one stood to one side.

"Not approaching too near, not standing too far, not clinging to that side, not holding to the other side either — thus that deity, having stood to one side, remained standing."

Why in this manner? Because of such considerations the deity stood thus, without coming too near or standing elsewhere; a great deity of power, coming and standing well-poised, mindful, reaches the human realm; and thereafter, in accordance with its purpose, proceeds further.

"Skilled in the welfare of the other world, skilled in overcoming death, skilled in the undying, skilled in overcoming Māra, skilled in the deathless" — in this manner, first explaining what should not be cultivated, it says: "Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise." But then, in the order stated by the elder, is it first the non-association with fools or the association with the wise that is more important? There is no one called a fool merely by birth, caste, or similar distinctions alone — they are known as fools by their characteristics from birth to birth. As the saying goes: "What is called the behavior of a fool is like that of a foolish child." For example, from ancient times, in the case of Devadatta the wicked one, Kokalika, and others like them — those who, like fish in the ocean, drifted about — they came to ruin. These are shown as fools. Those without shame and fear of wrongdoing, those who harm themselves and others through their conduct and speech, lead to destruction. Just as one who follows the wrong path falls off a great cliff, so those who follow foolish ones fall into great suffering; as it is said: "Even those who dwell near such fools, whether in a burning house or a house on fire, those who are afflicted, who are cut off..." "Do not associate with fools, do not listen to fools, do not live with fools,

What burden did you carry for Kassapa, O fool?

Thus, the Blessed One, having condemned in every way the association with fools as being no blessing, now praising the association with the wise, declared that associating with the wise is a blessing. Those called the wise are beings who have come to possess the ten wholesome courses of action beginning with abstaining from taking life, and they are known by these characteristics. As the saying goes, "Thus, O monks, one knows the marks of a wise person." Also, the eighty great disciples who had attained clear insight, as well as various others — Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Viḷīra, and Sarābha who assembled together — and Nimi the king, Ayosara the prince, and others such as these are also known as the wise. Just as a guard provides protection, just as a physician removes the fever of hunger and thirst and the burning of various afflictions, so too those who act according to one's words work for the benefit and welfare of all. As for people — gods and humans dwelling in this world, whether in the world of humans or the divine world or the blissful realm — it is told of the Elder Sāriputta that, surrounded by a great retinue, together with his companions, he attained Nibbāna. Thus the Blessed One, having praised the association with the wise in all respects, now, having praised the avoidance of fools and the association with the wise, and having praised the veneration of those worthy of veneration as a further quality worthy of practice, speaks of veneration as auspicious. Those worthy of veneration are: the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possessed of all virtues and qualities, the Pacceka-buddhas, and the Noble Ones. Even a material offering to these — flowers, garlands, jasmine-garlands and the like — is an auspicious gift. That is material veneration. How much more so the veneration of practice? Those who, following the precepts, the going for refuge, the undertaking of the training rules, keeping the Uposatha observances, being endowed with virtuous qualities, worship the Blessed One with virtues — who would deny the greatness of that worship? It would not be proper to say that one has paid the highest homage. As the Buddha said: "Whoever among the monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen lives practicing the Dhamma and its accompaniments, conducting themselves rightly, it is they who honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata with the highest homage." b In accordance with this, even the veneration paid by Pacceka-buddhas and Noble Ones is said to be auspicious. Also in the household context, veneration of mother, father, teachers, elders, husband, wife, and parents-in-law is auspicious and brings benefits such as long life and prosperity through the acquisition of good qualities. As it is said: "Those who undertake this wholesome practice among families and communities will prosper; those who promote and support these good qualities among people are themselves worthy of commendation." c Now as to what further aspects of auspiciousness are taught — it is said here: Avoiding fools, associating with the wise, and venerating those worthy of veneration — this is the highest blessing. Through the performance of deeds, consciousness arises; some arise being free from training, through the cultivation of unique perfections for a hundred thousand aeons together with many eons, great disciples arise; others, freed from training through the cultivation of perfections for a hundred thousand eons, become Paccekabuddhas; others, through four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons of cultivation of perfections together with a hundred thousand eons, become Fully Enlightened Buddhas.

Having taken the division of consciousness in this way, the purity of the four modes of conduct in virtue should be understood: for Paccekabuddhas it is purity relying on oneself; for Fully Self-Enlightened Buddhas and for Buddha's disciples, the purity relying on the Teaching or relying on Nibbāna is the basis—thus these attainments should be understood to arise variously according to conduct. "Having done merit before" means: having previously, in a past birth, aroused aspiration directed at a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a disciple of a Buddha — what is that, friends? Having seen a Buddha, or a disciple of a Buddha, assembled, having sought the lineage [of liberation], paying homage at the feet of an Arahant — this is called "having done merit before" by the wise. One who has previously planted roots of merit, being established in good roots, performing a wholesome deed without wavering, even giving up kingship like certain kings did — this is said to be "having done merit before," friends. "Perfecting the ends" means here: being established firmly in virtue regarding external conduct, approaching with devotion toward good conduct, being established in reverence toward the Teacher — this is called "perfecting the ends." What is this, friends? It means abandoning former defilements through the practice set forth in the true Dhamma teaching. Thus, by means of these four verses spoken as teaching, one who has done merit in the past is said to have "perfected the ends" — this is explained by the wise. Thus it should be understood accordingly.

Mangala Sutta Commentary.

Moreover, one who honors his parents who have borne him with affection, establishing them in virtue and in giving, that is the manner of repaying the kindness done by one's parents. By supporting them, protecting them, and establishing them well in the Dhamma, one accomplishes the welfare-blessing known as mangala. Among children, one who is born in that lineage, whether it be a son or a daughter, should look after the parents in the same way. Children are hard to find, as are good children. A son who is distant and a son who is near — in regard to such sons, there is the matter of mutual support and fellowship, and so forth. Thus, through good conduct, arranging the welfare related to the Dhamma is called mangala. For this reason the Blessed One said: "In five ways should a son support his parents." Also, on the matter of supporting the wife, the Blessed One declared in the Sigālovāda: "In five ways, O son of a good family, should a husband support his wife as a master: by honoring her, by not disrespecting her, by not being unfaithful, by granting her authority, and by providing adornments. When supported in these five ways by her husband as his master, O son of a good family, the wife shows compassion to her husband in five ways: she performs her duties well, she manages the household well, she is not unfaithful, she safeguards what has been gained, and she is skillful and diligent in all duties." This is one explanation. According to another method: Saṅgaha (support/sustenance) means providing for one's relatives on the proper and improper days, following local customs, and performing blessings on appropriate festival days when such are observed, and so forth, following the well-known methods, for both relatives' welfare according to the Dhamma and for one's own kin as well as for gods and other kin — this sustaining is to be understood as mangala. As stated in verse:

"One who supports his spouse and children righteously with virtue and devotion, nourishing them through the Dhamma — that one I call blessed (maṅgala)."

Orderly work (anākulā kammantā) means: work done at the proper time, in the proper manner, diligently, with the completion of one's undertakings, without quarrel, avoiding at all times improper actions, inappropriate work, dishonest dealing, and other unwholesome deeds; avoiding things like carelessness and theft in one's occupation. Whether for oneself or for one's family members, working skillfully and diligently in such occupations here in this very life is called mangala. Thus the Blessed One declared: "Appropriate action, diligence, these constitute right conduct," as follows:

"Not sleeping by day, delighting in diligence by night,
remaining ever mindful and skillful, dwelling in happiness.

Not too cold, not too hot, not sleeping too much,
thus performing one's varied duties, this indeed is called wealth."

And so forth. In this verse too, the duties toward mother and father, toward sons and daughters, toward companions of the householder and women overcome by desire — these are explained. Likewise various types of maidens associated with the householder's companions. Those who are known to mother and father among those to be respected. Women, indeed, are thus depicted. By this verse, those who honor their mothers and fathers are not to be despised.

Now, the giving described here as being given in reference to another — that which deprives others — is called giving that benefits others. These too are not blameworthy; they are not reproachable, not censurable. The explanation of the term proceeds thus: What is called "giving" is that which is offered for the sake of another — it is known as pure giving. Such giving produces benefit not from greed. Why is that? Because it is said: the giver gives for the sake of others. For those engaged in worldly and spiritual pursuits — laypeople and others pursuing conventional and higher goals — such giving is the means of attainment. As it is said: "The generous one is dear to many people, like a great tree in a park." This is to be reflected upon. Now, giving is twofold: material giving and Dhamma giving. Material giving has already been described. What belongs to this world and the next — for the welfare, happiness, and liberation of beings — that teaching given out of compassion for others is Dhamma giving. Of these two kinds of giving, that alone is the highest. Hence it is said:

"Giving of kindness exceeds Dhamma-giving in life,
Taste of kindness exceeds Dhamma-taste in life,
Joy in kindness exceeds Dhamma-joy in life,
The destruction of craving is the joy of kindness in life."

Now, as for material giving, the qualities of the noble ones have already been described. As for Dhamma giving, since it communicates the qualities of those with attainment and insight, it is noble indeed. As it is said: "Wherever, wherever one who wishes good, going from place to place, teaches the Dhamma for others' welfare — those become endowed with the attainment of insight, endowed with the attainment of insight."

Here, "ārati" (abstention) refers to internal inclination of the mind; "virati" (restraint) is cessation/ceasing. "Viramana" means refraining; that by which one abstains is called "virati." "Pāpa" (evil) means the unwholesome. Regarding "flesh," wherever meat or the drinking of liquor is spoken of, there "majjapāna" (strong drink) refers to restraint from intoxicants, i.e., non-heedlessness, and skillful dwelling in wholesome states — the remaining explanation should be understood as before. But here it should be understood thus: "Ārati" refers to the mind's mere turning away in disgust from an object; it is only mental. "Virati" refers to the abandonment, by body and speech, of killing and so forth as a type of action. This is of three kinds: abstention through opportunity (sampatta-virati), abstention through undertaking the precept (samādāna-virati), and abstention through eradication (samuccheda-virati).

Herein, when a person — for the sake of his own life, birth, clan, lineage, or for a monetary reason — refrains, in a fitting manner, from taking what is not given though it is proper to take it, or refrains from killing though he could, or acts similarly regarding the taking of life, this is called "sampatta-virati" (abstention arising due to circumstance). The abstention that arises through undertaking the training precepts is called "samādāna-virati" — for one who, having undertaken the precepts, from that day onward does not kill living beings even at the risk of his own life. "Samuccheda-virati" refers to the abstention belonging to one upon the noble path, for whom such restraint has become established as a matter of course.

"Pāpa" is explained thus: "Killing living beings, taking what is not given, misconduct in sexual desires, false speech... and so forth, these are to be understood in detail as given [in the texts]."

"Killing living beings, taking what is not given, false speech,
And going to others' wives — the wise do not praise these."

These, when summarized together, are the fourfold "kamma-kilesa" (defilements of action) classified as unwholesome; therefore they are "pāpa" (evil). All these, whether abstention (ārati) or restraint (virati), when accompanied by the four dreadful kinds of fear and arising at the time of such associated evil deeds as killing and so on, are called the "Great Ones" ("mahāla"). As it is said: "The noble disciple, a householder's son, who abstains from killing living beings..." and so on — this should be understood by following the Suttas accordingly.

Regarding intoxicants — previously mentioned as drinking liquor, etc. — abstention from intoxicating drinks and liquors is meant by "restraint from intoxicants." But one who indulges in intoxicating drink does not know what is beneficial, does not know the Dhamma; he may act against his own mother, and may harm even Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Noble Sangha...

Madhyagalu Commentary, page 89

[This page forms part of the Sinhala commentary (Atthakatha) on the Madhyaga/Middle teachings. The text is a scholastic commentary in classical Pali-Sinhala mixed style. A readable translation of the legible portions follows:]

One who acts in accordance with the teaching, having seen the Dhamma here itself in this very life, reaches calamity in the next life in the case of the heedless; but the restrained one, by calming those tendencies, does not fall into recklessness. This is how the "Middle Way" is to be understood. With regard to wholesome states, through heedfulness, by not being able to fully pursue wholesome things, through actions of non-attachment and actions of non-harmful conduct, freed from depression and withdrawn from it, not devoted, not pursued, not practiced in abundance, not accumulated — one of such nature who is slack and slackens in such heedlessness — this is called "heedlessness." The antidote to such heedlessness is to be understood as zeal and enthusiasm in wholesome states. Because it is the cause for attaining the deathless through the power of being devoted to wholesome practice, it is called the "Middle Way." As said — "For the heedful one, the path is clear" — and similarly "In heedfulness, the foremost" — and other such teachings are to be followed. Thus the way to suppress evil through wisdom and restraint in wholesome states is called heedfulness — this is the Middle Way. Those who hear this teaching will transcend [suffering]. This is the conclusion of the commentary on this section.

Now the word "garavo" (reverence) is defined: Reverence means the act of showing honor and esteem toward teachers, preceptors, the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, toward parents and other venerable persons — this is called reverence. The person who is reverent thinks: "Those worthy of reverence must be revered, those worthy of respect must be respected, those worthy of service must be served." By practicing in this way evenly toward those who are equal, and rightly toward those who are superior, the wholesome karma thus generated causes one to be born in a good world — not to fall into a lower realm. Thus it is asked: "In what teaching, to what extent, is this so?" — and the answer given is that this is the Middle Way. The word "nivaso" (dwelling) means: residing, settling, establishing oneself in a place — whether one settles in a city, a village, or a forest — by dwelling in a place endowed with good qualities and virtuous associations, wholesome conditions arise. This is the Middle Way called "dwelling." Thus "proper dwelling" — as shown in the footnote references below.

Commentary on the Discourse on Blessings (Maṅgala Sutta)

The person who, though having a little wealth for subsistence, does not give it to others out of forgetfulness is said to be "one living in a householder's life not according to the Dhamma." Furthermore, when someone falls ill, if there is a person who, having taken oil, applies it, and in dependence on that one's assistance the sick one recovers, and his sickness subsides through the application of oil, if those who are so helped later show gratitude by associating with and serving that person -- such a one is said to be "one who lives rightly in the religious life of giving."

In another case, there is a woodworker who makes various things for others, dividing his time between them. His conduct is such that illness afflicts him from various causes, yet there is said to be one who gives hospitality meritoriously thus: "This is for one who has given hospitality, in dependence on which this benefit arises; may he seek and gain [something] accordingly" -- so it is said, and such a one is regarded as one who truly follows the duty of hospitality towards a woodworker.

This is to be remembered as such. One who has reflected and corrected himself and acts rightly is said to be "one who dwells rightly in the religious life of giving" accordingly. In this manner, with various reasons, it should be understood as consisting in these dispositions. It is said: this [giving] is the cause for a stable state, the cause for attaining a good destiny, the supporting condition for the development of the Noble Path, and the very foundation of speech and conduct well done -- thus it should be understood as "a blessing." As it is said: "Giving which is not accompanied by the right cause is the beginning of good speech and conduct" and so forth.

"Done with gratitude" means: having received benefit from one or from many, remembering it again and again without forgetting, bringing it to mind for the sake of the people; and furthermore, even without any particular reward, this itself becomes the condition. Thus the Buddha has spoken on this matter, and it should likewise be understood that even for those who have benefited, a reciprocal kindness/service is appropriate.

Because it is the cause for serving at the right time, serving the wise, this is called "a blessing." As it is said: "Monks, there are these two kinds of individuals hard to find in the world" -- timely listening to the Dhamma means that the mind becomes devoted at such a time, without agitation, with desire aroused for it; but if one is not inattentive, then at that very time the hindrances are removed -- this is "listening to the Dhamma." Further, when on the day following the full moon one listens to the Dhamma at the time of Dhamma-preaching, this is called "listening to the Dhamma at the right time." Venerable Ānuruddha has said thus: "Friends, we who dwell together in harmony, delighting in each other, without disputing, blending like milk and water, looking upon each other with eyes of affection, dwell thus." At the time of listening to the Dhamma, one who is skilled and wise, intent on his own welfare and that of others, should be understood as "one who listens to the Dhamma at the right time," as taught: "Of those who, at the right time, practice insight into the arisen Dhamma" and so on. In this way, listening to the Dhamma at the right time, through the cause of removing the five hindrances, by means of the four requisites of robes and so forth, is the cause of various benefits -- thus it should be understood as "a blessing." As it has been further said: "Monks, there are these things which, when practiced and developed by a noble disciple, listening to the Dhamma at the appropriate time with an undistracted mind gives rise to these benefits: he listens to the Dhamma he has not heard before, he clarifies the Dhamma already heard, he removes doubt, his view becomes straight, and his mind becomes serene" -- the benefits of listening to the Dhamma are explained thus in detail. Further it is said: "Whatever beings there are, possessed of perception or without distinction of perception, whoever attains calm and clear understanding and tastes the flavor of the Dhamma, overcomes thirst, is freed from fear, and gains the supreme bliss" -- this too is said, and "these are the Dhammas which, when heard at the right time, lead to and produce excellent fruits accordingly."

Here, in brief, with regard to the teaching suitable for a single occasion — "effort" (kappo) means the practice of the holy life (brahmacariya), or the conduct of the Brahma-like ones, called "holy conduct" (brahmacariya = sevariya). The vision of hearing the Noble Ones is called "the vision of the higher hearing." As for "the vision of the hearing of the Noble Ones," there are cases where even that is not well understood. The arising of exertion toward Nibbana, the practice leading to it, is called "the practice conducive to Nibbana." The explanation ends there, this is to be understood accordingly.

"Effort" (kappa) refers to a monk; the effort applied toward the stimulation of the senses by objects such as deities, or toward making the mind pliant, is called effort, since it is through this uniform exertion that one is said to be "ardent" (ātāpī). This is auspicious because it leads to higher deities.

"Holy life" (brahmacariya) refers to abstention from sexual intercourse; this meaning is intended, as in such statements as "One living the holy life is a Brahma-farer" and so forth; "Said with reference to the Blessed One's own practice of the holy life," and so on, as appropriate. "I shall fulfil this training precept as long as I live, for the sake of this very holy life that has been the means of deliverance for me, so declared the Teacher"; thus it is said, "This one indeed is foremost in the holy life among the practice of restraint, being heedful, he abides" — thus elsewhere it is stated. But here, with regard to seeing by hearing the Noble Ones, the wholesome factor (kusala) that is established through the remaining elements, by such and such causation based on the nourishing factors, is to be understood as auspicious.

"The vision of the higher hearing" refers to what is spoken of concerning the cessation of the round of rebirth for a youth or a maiden established in the Dhamma, this being called auspicious because it serves as means to cut off samsaric suffering. "The practice conducive to Nibbana" means this: whatever leads to Nibbana for the Arahant, being completely extinguished with respect to those defilements which, when quenched, bring about cessation — that is called Nibbana; and the cause for reaching that is called the practice conducive to it. But for others, it is accomplished through the seeing which comes from the hearing of the Noble Ones alone — hence it is called "practice conducive to Nibbana." Thus, in this verse, effort and the holy life are to be understood as the Noble Auspicious ones.]

Having abandoned unwholesome tendencies through the quality of virtue, and having trained in the practice of restraint as taught by the Teacher, following in the tradition of the disciples and preceptors — remaining unattached and controlled, one guards the training rules. With contentment, practicing restraint in the sense faculties, having abandoned harmful conduct toward others, possessing complete virtue, refraining from actions that are blameworthy, one applies oneself to the development of insight. Seeing through wisdom the nature of phenomena, achieving liberation through purification of virtue, then purification of mind, then purification of view — these seven purifications lead to final liberation. Through the culmination of noble insight-knowledge, the seventh purification of knowledge-and-vision of the path is attained. This leads to the attainment of arahantship, the realization of Nibbana. Just as one who stands on the peak of a mountain can see all around, so too the one who has thus attained — free from sorrow, free from passion, free from delusion — becomes one who has transcended all. Thus it is said: "The one who is like this is noble in all respects, and in all respects goes beyond suffering — such is the meaning of this Mangala."

The Commentary called Sarattha-samuccaya, being the explanation by way of the noble method — the Commentary on the Maha-Mangala Sutta — is hereby concluded.

"Why should that which you honor with offerings by day and by night not protect you?" The meaning is: the benefit of performing offerings is indeed the protection and guarding of human beings. As the Blessed One said to Ananda: "Whatever excellent things there are, whether belonging to oneself or not belonging to oneself..." - thus it should be understood that things belonging to oneself are called "self," and things not belonging to oneself are called "not-self" possessions; otherwise, in the other sense, there would be a contradiction. Previously, this was stated as a summary; now the detailed explanation is given. "Giving gifts" (dānapatīnam) means donors, i.e., a single word with alternate case forms used variably. Here "gifts and donations" refer to the acts of giving. "Discerning" (vicakkhaṇā) refers to wise ones. "Taking as object" means apprehending through the sense faculties. This is proclaimed. Thus it is said that the fruit obtainable from gifts given to such persons is the attainment of liberation — this very attainment is declared to be the great reward — this [applies] to persons who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) only.
