This was said with reference to Anuradhapura. [It describes] pure, discerning conduct free from faults, proper conduct in observing moral precepts, proper conduct in wandering about, and proper conduct regarding knowledge of lodgings, all accomplished with the same intention. One should not transgress improperly—bodily grasping through improper physical conduct, verbally grasping through improper speech, and mentally grasping through improper mental conduct should be avoided.

Here, "bodily grasping" means: when a monk enters among a group of fellow monastics and his body or conduct is unsuitable in that assembly—how is this? Here it is said regarding the fivefold fault of posture—bowing improperly, and so forth—or conduct that is inappropriate to skillful bodily deportment, or inappropriate to the rules of training followed by other monastics. Regarding food, when eating with the Sangha, if one is not mindful of the proper measure or order of seating, or if one disturbs the arrangement of seats meant for elders according to seniority, or if one, while washing hands or receiving water, acts out of turn disturbing others young or old—these are examples of bodily impropriety that disturbs the harmony of the community when entering among fellow monks. This is called bodily impropriety.

As for verbal impropriety: when one speaks words unsuitable to the occasion, interrupting elders who are speaking, or raises unrelated or improper topics when entering an assembly of fellow monastics—this disturbs proper order and is called improper verbal conduct, such as saying "what have I eaten," "what shall I do," or similar remarks out of place.

As for mental impropriety: having thoughts contrary to proper conduct of body and speech towards one's companions is called mental impropriety.

Thus one guards body, speech, and mind so as not to offend companions through improper bodily, verbal, or mental conduct; this protects the harmony of the fellowship when living among others.

Further, one whose mind does not become joyful [at improper things], nor sorrowful without cause, who does not exult excessively nor become despondent, who remains even-minded towards those who are joyful or sorrowful—of such a one it is said that he dwells evenly amid happiness and suffering alike, without attachment or aversion. Thus the Blessed One declared the state of such even-mindedness to be the proper abiding.

One who wishes to attain the state of a non-returner, who is desirous of such practice and devoted to it, and who wishes to restrain certain things even now in this very life—such a monk who refrains from wrongdoing and avoids both the misconduct of body and speech, following the Buddha's teaching rightly, is said to walk in the path taught by the Enlightened One.

Just as one who has given up attachment is called "one who guards," so too the mind becomes like space. In that same way, by means of "the light of the world of congregation," one contemplates with the mind. The growth of mind expands beyond all measure, beyond immeasurable limits, as is said. Above, there is no grasping at formless existence; likewise, there is no grasping at sense-sphere existence; likewise, the fine-material sphere existence is also not grasped. Regarding freedom from obstruction and its limits, as is stated: a being designated as "bounded" arises; as is declared, it is also said that within and without the barriers there is the dissolution of obstructions through the release of those barriers. For one who dwells without obstruction, whether human or non-human, whether for that one who moves inwardly or outwardly, the mind being freed from obstruction does not dwell in the condition of obstruction. In the ultimate sense, through this approach, one proceeds onward. In this context, the full mastery of the foremost among all beings — with a mind that is immeasurable — means the mind is unlimited among all worlds, growing without obstacle. So what can obstruct it? Going up or going down is only in name. 152 Sāratthasamuccaya

The Supreme One (Bhagavā), by whose going forth and dwelling among beings in the cycle of existence, through causes such as those enumerated — namely, by wisdom, understanding, mindfulness, and knowledge — on account of such reasons:

"The word 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) — the word Bhagavā is supreme,
By reason of reverence and veneration, he is called Bhagavā."

For those reasons, one should recollect that Bhagavā. Contemplating all beings with complete and encompassing vision of the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-proclaimed (svākkhāto) by the Blessed One — well-proclaimed! One should recollect the Dhamma." One should recollect the Dhamma. Why so? Because from the well-proclaimed (svākkhāto) quality onward, the Dhamma — as taught through precepts and so forth — even to a householder provides a basis. And so through the recollection of the Dhamma, it is not divided; and compared to the Dhamma of the world, it is superior. The well-proclaimed Dhamma, as summarized from beginning through its entirety, is complete and not deficient, and fully practiced leads to liberation from defilements. Unlike the teachings of the world which are subject to distortion: these teachings of the world are near to distortion, while the Dhamma here — through these gradual trainings — maintains its character without distortion and without confusion.

The Dhamma of the world, on the other hand, suited to nibbāna in its own nature, being completely practiced through the path that leads to nibbāna, and through the stages of attainment, through the full training — the well-proclaimed Dhamma (svākkhāto) is distinguished. Nibbāna, being calmly and moderately described in its character, is visible here and now (sandiṭṭhiko) as something that the Noble One realizes personally, is directly visible, not delayed, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. So too, one who has right view (sammādiṭṭhi) achieves it for themselves by their own effort in this very world. Thus this Dhamma, being seen and understood, is a cause for confidence. And so the one who has attained right view (sammādiṭṭhika), attaining it thus, verifying it in successive stages, attains it again and again through right view, attains the seen and verifiable, and so the Dhamma is confirmed as directly visible and well-attained.

The supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), through the occasion of meditation-attainment and through the occasion of functional activity, makes itself apparent in this way. For Nibbana is such that, just as that Arahant who has seen it directly sees it as directly visible (sanditthika). Therefore, in one respect, it is "not a matter of time" (akalika) — not something belonging to a particular time in the sense of waiting for a season to bear fruit in a later existence; rather, in the sense that when one practices, the fruit arises right then and there, in that very moment. But in another sense, one might ask: what is "timely" (kalika)? That is the wholesome Dhamma (kusala-dhamma) of the mundane world. For ordinary good deeds, unlike supramundane ones, are indeed timely — they ripen in a future time and place. This has been stated here as an example. Moreover, because the supramundane Dhamma does not belong to the category of "timely" things such as pleasant and unpleasant seasonal experiences, it is therefore called "akalika" (timeless).

Now, one may ask: in how many ways is the Arahant's quality to be seen and known directly? Because of knowledge and purity — just as gold that is pure and free of dross is fit to be fashioned into whatever form, so too this Dhamma: why? Because of the absence of ignorance. Just as when ignorance is removed and knowledge stands firm, like the sky cleared of clouds, filled with the full moon's light — the wise one who is pure and cleansed: thus, because of knowledge and because of purity, the Arahant's quality is to be seen in both these ways. Regarding "Opanayika" (leading inward): it means "leading toward" — from the time of its arising, through the practice of meditation, it continuously leads the practitioner forward, drawing him ever closer. In this way, the supramundane Dhamma leads inward to Nibbana. It is "opanayika" in the sense that through functional activity it draws one to liberation, to the Arahant state. The factors of enlightenment (bojjhangas) are so called because of their nature as things by which one is enlightened, or because they lead to enlightenment. As it is said: "Monks, at the time of the arising of the eye (vision) among beings, at the arising of the Dhamma-light, at the arising of the Perfectly Enlightened One among beings, the arising of the factors of enlightenment comes to pass" — this and more is stated as the proper teaching. "Bhāvitā" (developed) means: they arise endowed with the qualities of seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment, by abandoning the opposing states; "bahulīkatā" (repeatedly practiced) means cultivated by repeated arising; "abhisambodhāya" means for the purpose of the noble full understanding; "nibbānāya" means for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna; "saṃvattanti" means they lead (thereto). The meaning of "abhisambodhāya" and so forth is: as for these bojjhangas, their characteristic activity is known by that name. That which functions as the basis for insight (vipassanā) belongs to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), while that which arises at the time of insight (vipassanā) used as the foundation belongs to the supramundane. "Sakkhe satatikiṭi" means: they are properly established together in conjunction. In the same way all the bojjhangas are present together with sati (mindfulness), and so on for the rest. "Samudākinṇokātiṭi" means: by the method of fulfilling all the various skillful means, they fill everything completely. As stated before with respect to the arising: "bhāvikā" means — for that which has not yet arisen, causing it to arise; for that which has arisen, bringing it to perfection — through appropriate attention (yoniso manasikāra) along with wholesome factors such as energy and so forth, it is cultivated. Regarding the bojjhanga of dhamma-vicaya (investigation of states): it is well stated thus — "Monks, at a time when the mind is active and alert, that is the time for developing the bojjhanga of dhamma-vicaya" — as properly taught. "Bhāvikā" means: for what has not arisen, causing it to arise; for what has arisen, bringing it to fulfillment through appropriate attention together with clarity and discernment and thorough investigation, and it is cultivated in that way. Regarding the bojjhanga of pīti (rapture): it is well stated thus — "Monks, at a time when the mind is active and alert, that is the time for developing the bojjhanga of pīti" — as properly taught. "Bhāvikā" means: for what has not arisen, causing it to arise; for what has arisen, bringing it to fulfillment through attention to rapture-inducing objects and so forth, cultivated in various ways. Regarding the bojjhanga of passaddhi (tranquility):

Commentary on the Development of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhanga-bhavana-vannana)

Regarding the characteristic of "fully attaining the enlightenment factor of concentration" — the phrase "at whatever time the mind is uplifted" means: "at that time, the enlightenment factor of tranquility should be developed." The word "developed" refers to what has arisen; by fulfilling the development of tranquility of body and mind through wise attention, nourishment of the wholesome, and such other conditions — thus it is said to be "developed." Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration — the phrase "at whatever time the mind is uplifted" means "at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration should be developed." "Properly stated" means: for what has not yet arisen, for bringing it to arise; for what has already arisen, for its full development through wise attention, nourishment, and other such means — thus it is cultivated. Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity — "at whatever time the mind is uplifted, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity should be developed" — thus it is stated. "Developed" means: bringing unarisen equanimity to arise, and fulfilling the development of what has arisen.

These seven enlightenment factors, when developed, lead to the attainment of arahantship. Just as the wheel-treasure, foremost among the treasures of the wheel-turning monarch, rolls through many levels of existence and illuminates the path — so too does the Dhamma-body, like the jewel-treasure that lights up the darkness — so too does the energy-enlightenment factor, like the elephant-treasure that leads the way — so too does the rapture-enlightenment factor, like the wish-fulfilling gem that illuminates with inner light — so too does the tranquility-enlightenment factor, like the woman-treasure that brings peace and comfort — so too does the concentration-enlightenment factor, like the householder-treasure that brings beings together in harmony — and thus all these are comparable to the treasures of the wheel-turning king. The enlightenment factor of equanimity is the foremost among all of these.

The word "Panita" (noble/excellent) means that which is unsurpassed in arising from the noble; even for those seated among the lowly, it is called "Panita" by name. "Sabbasankharasamelo" and so forth — those same feelings apply; "Sabbasankharasamelo" means the cessation of all formations, the disappearance of passion. Even in the Long Collection, the statement proceeds in the same way: "Sabbasankharasamelo" — and so on — thereafter, through the cessation of craving and thirst, Nibbana is attained. Thus, having obtained it, one does not return to existence; Nibbana is called Nibbana in and of itself. Therefore, "Sabbasankharasamelo" and what follows are called "name" (nama). The explanation of the passage is this: Nibbana is the highest, most peaceful and noble; therefore "Sabbasankharasamelo" — and so on — Nibbana. That which is called "Sabbasankharasamelo" and so on refers to the unconditioned element; that is the element of dispassion, the element of cessation, and as all formations cease, it is called Sabbasankharasamelo. In this context, the four upadhis (attachments) are: the upadhi of sensual pleasures, the upadhi of the aggregates, the upadhi of defilements, and the upadhi of volitional formations. Whatever is born thereby, one experiences the gratification of sensual pleasures — but from that very gratification arises suffering, danger, and bondage; and from that, one does not escape. All the phenomena of the world — their arising, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them — these are seen clearly through insight. And thus it is said:

"Having pervaded the entire world with the flooding of the entire world,
through disenchantment with the entire world, one is not attached to the entire world."

This passage elaborates on the practice of mindfulness of breathing: "When one knows the long in-breath as a long in-breath, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and awareness, pīti (joy/rapture) is experienced throughout the body. When one knows the long out-breath as a long out-breath, with the short in-breath and out-breath, experiencing the whole body through the in-breath and out-breath, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and awareness, pīti is experienced. Through attending, knowing, fully understanding, entering, dwelling, overcoming, fully releasing with perception, striving, noting mindfully, establishing, concentrating, and fully knowing with wisdom — through these, one experiences pīti (rapture) fully. Thus pīti is experienced throughout."

By this same principle, the remaining terms are to be understood down to the last. This special distinction should be known: in what sense is sukha (pleasure/happiness) fully experienced? It is experienced because it is known, perceived, and felt. As for sukha itself: "It is called sukha because it gives happiness; it is called sukha because it is pleasant." Thus by analogy with pīti, sukha is to be understood similarly.

Furthermore, the experience of vedanā (feeling/sensation) is to be comprehended in its various aspects: as pīti is experienced through the bodily factor, so too sukha is experienced in its own characteristic way. The meditator, having fully attended to the object and having understood it through direct knowledge, comes to experience cessation. He who meditates on the mental formations, knows them directly, and experiences them through the mind — he comes to know feeling in all its aspects. Similarly, through concentration and insight, with the arising of joy and the stilling of the bodily formation, the meditator using the in-breath and out-breath as the basis for the mind's object, attains and dwells in joy, pleasure, and equanimity. Through insight-knowledge and concentration-knowledge together, having fully comprehended the object, the mind becomes unified and blissful. Thus, using insight as the means and taking the bodily formation as the mind's object, one fully achieves the goal of concentration.

"Pleasant" — therefore said with sweetness; among the recently-arisen teachings it is said that this very sutta should be recited, for the deities, hearing this sutta, would move about satisfied in that very place. After the discourse concluded, a hundred-thousand koṭis of deities attained arahantship, and [others] attained the fruit of stream-entry; thus it is said, out of affection and pleasure for the deities, [this] was said:—

It is said that in the region of Koṭipabbata, in the Nāga realm, there dwelt a certain female deity. In one world-system a certain [being] in another plane recites this sutta; at the conclusion of the sutta, the deities together raise a great shout of approval. "Who is reciting?" they said; "Venerable sir, it is a deity." "For whose sake is this applause given?" [they asked]. "Venerable sir, sitting in that great forest-grove, [the Buddha] on the full-moon day spoke this sutta — thus we say it was so received." Taking up that being's intention, "In one single life, might I too attain that state, by the strength of what cause does this come about?" they asked. "Why so, Venerable sir? For truly, the deities, declaring 'thus has he gone,' then — how can this matter be explained?" "Why is it, Venerable sir, that the deities dwelling in that great forest are in this condition — are they liberated, or still bound? Among the great assembly of deities, some deities who have come from Jambudīpa, desiring to hear the teaching here, having come to this very island to the Jambu-tree region, wishing to listen, approach there." Thus, for the sake of those deities of the great assembly gathering to hear the teaching, in due order, proceeding — [the account describes] the great multitude's shining radiance, like a golden hue, drinking in the water with delight, free from suffering and sorrow — "do you, O deity, dwell afar off like this?" "What should be done now, Venerable sir? Determining to teach the Dhamma in this great forest, viewing it thus, they look upon and reflect upon one another's radiant bodies, on that very day." "It is said that a hundred-thousand koṭis of deities attained arahantship that day — did you yourself also attain that?" "No, Venerable sir." "Did those who attained the state of non-returner receive such praise?" "No, Venerable sir." "Did those who attained once-returning receive such praise?" "No, Venerable sir. Rather, it is said that the deities honor even one who has attained stream-entry." "Was it then said, 'On the day one attains stream-entry, their relatives offer unprecedented worship'?" "Yes, even so it is." He then asked, "But, O deity, is it possible for you to go there now?" "It is not possible, Venerable sir, to describe the whole matter — permit me to just show you a glimpse." Then, by a small opening, light shone forth like sunlight piercing through, as if by the vision of the moon arising — thus the deity, out of diligence, filled the entire womb-world with light.

The sutta [concludes]: "This is dear and pleasant to the deities" — thus is the Great Commentary.

End of the Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta, in the collection belonging to the fourth chapter [division] of the Sārārthasamuccaya.

One who is not protected by envy does not sleep peacefully. Because of sensual passion and ill-will, through wrong livelihood, one is brought to ruin. This verse, rooted in the explanation of envy, is stated as having ruin as its basis.

Commentary on the Alavaka Sutta.

It is said that at a certain time, on the new moon dark fortnight day, while the matter concerning the junior monk at the residence was in progress, [the Blessed One] approaching with mindfulness of conduct, out of compassion for the welfare [of the yakkha], dwelt in the dwelling of that fierce yakkha.

Now, it is asked: did the Blessed One himself go and dwell near the base of the dwelling of the yakkha Alavaka, or did he merely stay there? It is explained thus: he dwelt there. For indeed, for the sake of benefiting that yakkha, the Blessed One, out of compassion, went and stayed in that dwelling. At that time Alavaka had gone to a meeting of yakkhas; then two gatekeepers of Alavaka's dwelling, by name, approached the Blessed One and asked where he might spend the night and whether anyone might cause him trouble. One said: "If the Blessed One desires to stay one night in Alavaka's dwelling, that is not proper, for that yakkha does not even pay respect to his own mother and father, how then could he show respect to the Blessed One residing there?" Another said: "He will not cause any obstruction — let the Blessed One be allowed to stay one night there." They disputed in this way. So one went and informed Alavaka of the matter, and asked him to come, since the Blessed One wished to stay in his dwelling that night. Thus informed, Alavaka's companion likewise urged him onward. The Blessed One, having entered the dwelling and prepared to spend the night, sat radiant, having the signs and marks of a great being, blazing with excellent light. Seeing this, the female yakkhas approached and, worshipping, praised the Blessed One, requesting the Dhamma — observing moral precepts, honoring with offerings — thus they dwelt in happiness without doing any wrong, in a manner consistent with virtuous practice. Hearing of this, in due course Alavaka's attendants went forth and reported it diligently to him, saying: "The Blessed One has come and is residing in the dwelling." Hearing this, Alavaka, angered and provoked, resolved that he must act, and set out accordingly to confront him.

Commentary on the Discourse of Alavaka
Notes.

After the departure of the one described in the preceding commentary on the discourse, this is the commentary on it. Thus having been described in the sections above, it is also described in the sections on Vaslu. How did it arise? The Blessed One, while dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove in the monastery of Anathapindika, was going about teaching the world, and having caused Kasi-Bharadvaja the brahmin to take refuge and undertake the precepts, he gave teaching as was right at the proper time, so that Bharadvaja came to know the Dhamma. Having taken refuge, having received the going for refuge, they undertook the training. The brahmin then accepted the teaching of Dharma. He taught it well. Having then considered thoroughly, the Blessed One proceeded to show the Maha-Alavaka commentary in sequence. The Blessed One, having spoken in connection with the beginning such as Sutta-collection, gave the description. By whom and at what time was this discourse of Alavaka delivered? — whatever was described there is described here. As it is said: That brahmin came with his retinue to pay homage; Alavaka, named as such, addressed [it] — coming from Karamaja, then proclaimed the discourse of Alavaka; dwelling there in that very place, and concerning dwelling in the place as described, at that place, as the commentary states — in that dwelling the very commentary was produced; the dwelling being fully described, and the dwelling brought together — likewise was proclaimed. Having spiritually accomplished it, the Alavaka discourse was fully taught. The householders accordingly having heard it, and accepting the going for refuge and taking the precepts accordingly, the whole assembly accepted [the teaching].

This page appears to be from a Sinhala commentary (atthakatha) tradition, discussing the term "manasikara" (attention/mental engagement). The text explains that manasikara (attention) serves to direct the mind appropriately, describing how it functions in the context of hearing the Dhamma, retaining teachings, and properly orienting the mental faculties. The passage discusses the role of wise attention in both earlier and later stages of practice, and how it relates to the abandoning of wrong views and the cultivation of correct understanding. The text further elaborates on how this attention functions in relation to individuals of different temperaments and capacities, and how the Brahmin's role is discussed in relation to these teachings. The final paragraph discusses how on the following day the Brahmin came and, after being instructed, departed having understood the Dhamma, with the teaching being imparted in a way suited to his nature.

This page (231) from the Suttatthakatha commentary is written in a highly specialized Pali-Sinhala scholastic idiom. The script is partially damaged or faded in several places, making full translation difficult. The legible portions convey the following:

Even one who is aged and weakened, out of compassion, speaks words of value; the army does not act according to what has been instructed, thus it is not properly cared for. The notion is that whether one writes with one's hand or through a scribe or by any other means, one must communicate. Among the rest, by whatever means discourse is opened. Through the combination of various ascetic practices and disciplines, whatever one knows — whether through the living teaching or through the understanding of doctrine — it is made manifest. Among those who are learned, one should reflect: this is the deeper meaning of the teaching as it has been handed down. Those who hear it in the assembly, through the spoken word, come to understand what had not been understood before. Thus through a certain kind of reflection, the evil qualities — wrong-going, wrong intention, the paths of transgression — are examined. As it is said: "Through wrong-going of mind — through wrong courses of body, speech, and mind — evil deeds accumulate." By examining this, the bad accumulation is understood. Thus through proper consideration, the roots of unwholesome conduct are cut off: through wrongness in multitude, through wrongness in accumulation. By wisdom, one who had not seen comes to see; the unseen becomes known, and the merit of understanding arises.

The second paragraph discusses a great being who, having gone forth, in the time of the great assembly, in the higher congregation, with the higher understanding, in the midst of the assembly, reflects on proper conduct. Not seeing the higher principle, the being contemplates: "How may I act rightly?" Through proper practice and through following instruction from a teacher, illness is healed. Not yielding to pleasure, not given to distraction, the merit of proper restraint becomes apparent.

This page is from a Pali commentary text with Sinhala explanations. The passage discusses the concepts of who is truly a "vasala" (outcaste) and who is truly a "brahmana" (brahmin), drawing from the teachings of the Buddha (Bhagava).

The text explains: The Buddha, having taught the discourse on the outcaste, makes clear that it is not by birth that one becomes an outcaste or a brahmin, but by one's actions (kamma). One does not become an outcaste merely through birth, nor does one become a brahmin through birth; rather, through impure actions one becomes an outcaste, and through pure actions one becomes a brahmin. Just as one cannot judge a person as an outcaste or brahmin merely by looking at them, so too it is through their deeds that one is truly assessed.

The text continues to illustrate this point with examples: just as it is rare and difficult to be born in a noble family, similarly it is rare to find genuine virtue. The passage refers to various social classes — brahmins, warriors, merchants, and others — noting that in the human world of Jambudipa, those who make proper use of their birth and conduct themselves virtuously may ascend even to the divine realms, and through the culmination of their virtuous practice may attain to the Brahma world.

The text then proceeds to a narrative example involving a certain brahmin and a woman named Kira, referring to events in a city, mentioning a sibling, and various circumstances of livelihood and life, though portions of the text toward the bottom of the page become difficult to read clearly.

This page (numbered 235) is from a Pali commentary text (Suttatthakatha) written in Sinhala script. The passage describes a narrative scene as follows:

In that city, the son of Suriyaka (a wealthy merchant's son) set out to a park with a great retinue to play, accompanied by fifteen or sixteen young attendants as beautiful and lovely in form as a deity. A young woman known as Ditthimajjhilika, who was said to be of striking appearance and very attractive, came to his attention. Having seen her and been captivated by her beauty, he became bound to her. That day, having risen early in the morning, he looked out from his dwelling, saw a man being bound and led away toward the outskirts of the city, and heard talk of the road to the charnel ground. As he watched, the prisoner was being led away by men, away from the city. He asked, "Who is that?" Someone replied, "That is so-and-so." He thought: "Men, let us go and see this." Among those nearby were physicians, surgeons, attendants of various kinds, and householders, each one giving a reply in turn. Then arose a question: is this park the common property of all, or does it belong only to the Brahmins? It is the common property of all. Thus, since it is common to all, people enter it. But the Brahmins claim it as theirs. Being led thus into the park, the Brahmin's son watched and reflected. He saw the corpse being brought in, and thought: men, what is the use of attending to this? So he did not go further. The Brahmin's son had two portions of meat sent, and two portions of rice prepared. He did not go further. Thus returning home, that Brahmin woman who was his mother, on account of that sin, became an obstacle to the Ditthimajjhilika quarter. So, due to that fault, her punishment was carried out. Thus, by the effort of prince Bhatiyakumara, with the help of Matabhasa, bringing provisions, he reached that very day to the Ditthimajjhilika quarter. And so at that same moment, according to that account, he arrived there.

A man, standing on the full-moon night, gazing up at the sky, worshipping the orb [of the moon], noticed a great noble form in the sky. People thought it was something born of wonder. Gradually, coming and seeing day after day, they noticed that there was a woman's form in the sky. He thought: "I should go and bring this radiant one down and make her my wife." Thus that great man, seeing the lady of the sky dwelling there, approached her. She, too, being pleased, came down. He invited her respectfully, and so she entered his house. The house thereafter became known by a certain name. People came to see her, and the crowd was great. She entered with reverence. The Brahmin proclaimed: "This is my mother, born from the sky!" The people of the city honored the radiant one of the sky with golden ornaments and great processions. They led her in a great circumambulation of the city, adorned the city as if for a festival, and proclaimed to her that great noble form. Then they said: "For as long as good fortune lasts, we will keep this image." So a son was born to them at that pavilion. On a certain day, that young son, who had been born in the pavilion, cried out with desire. A Brahmin had come bringing gifts and honors befitting a son. The Brahmin gave the child many things to guard him. The child, being unable to accept them, gave them away to the Brahmin. The Brahmin said: "I give and give again, yet he gives it back" — seeing the Brahmin give things to others, and thinking "I will do whatever is commanded," he tried to settle the matter of the son's inheritance. "From where have you come, dwelling in beauty,

This page (253) is from the commentary on the Kasi-bharadvaja Sutta (Kasibharadvaja-suttavannana).

The text is a Pali commentary explaining the discourse between the Buddha and the brahmin Kasibharadvaja. The commentary discusses the following themes:

The brahmin Kasibharadvaja, having heard the teaching, reflects on the nature of "Kasi" (the field/plowing metaphor used by the Buddha). The text explains how faith, energy, and mindfulness serve as the tools of the spiritual farmer: just as a farmer plows a field with implements and seed, the practitioner cultivates the path with virtue, effort, and concentration. The commentary notes that suffering in its various forms — suffering as pain, suffering as conditioned existence, and suffering as change — is to be understood clearly.

The brahmin, having heard the Dhamma teaching, comes to understand that just as the land of Kasi belongs to all who cultivate it rightly, so too the teaching belongs to all who practice it — whether brahmin, warrior, merchant, or laborer. All who take up the practice share equally in this "field."

The text then goes on to discuss the brahmin's conversion: having understood the teaching, he becomes a follower. The commentary elaborates on the qualities of the "great being" (mahāsatta) and the nature of renunciation and non-attachment, explaining that the one who truly understands the Dhamma abandons clinging and attains peace.

This page (p. 259) is from the Saccavibhanga-suttannavannana (Commentary on the Discourse on the Analysis of Truth).

The text begins with a passage attributed to the Buddha: "Just as, monks, even an immeasurable [amount of] cow-dung has an immeasurable [number of] roots, hairs, and so forth, so too, monks, I, being immeasurable, did not reach even a fraction of those Arahants." It continues explaining that those who have not yet attained the state of Arahantship still fall into faults. The commentary then invokes the names of Sariputta and Moggallana as great exemplars among the disciples.

The text goes on to discuss the noble truths (sacca): suffering (dukkha), its origin (samudaya), its cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga) — explaining how attachment to sensual pleasures (kama) gives rise to suffering, and how freedom from such attachment leads toward liberation.

It states that for all the remaining passages the same method of interpretation applies. In all cases, through the various kinds of wisdom, the one meaning is obtained. Though they are called by different names, the meaning is the same. Likewise, even the earlier portions, through the various kinds of wisdom, the one meaning is obtained. The discourse is concluded with a purification of truth and a synopsis passage.

The closing verse section reads:

"To the community of monks endowed with virtue, the foremost one taught the Dhamma; by means of the true teaching adorned with good speech and knowledge, may this merit reach all beings throughout the world, and may they be freed from suffering."

The section heading at the end marks the conclusion of the Saccavibhangasutta commentary within the Ekuttaranikaya Parisishta-sangaha (Appendix Collection), with standard concluding benedictory verses.
